title: why 108
hookLine: a boy pushed off his father's lap, a sage's mantra, and the beads that count it
carry: count what you want to keep

cards: A little prince named Dhruva tries to climb onto his father the king's lap, and his stepmother stops him. Only her son sits there, she says. If you want that seat, go and pray to God.
Dhruva runs to his own mother, Suniti, in tears. She doesn't fight back. She tells him: she's right about one thing.
Turn to God. So the small boy walks into the forest. On the way he meets the sage Narada, who tries to send him home.
When Dhruva won't go, Narada gives him a mantra: om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, a bow to the Lord. Dhruva sits by the river Yamuna and says it, again, and again, and again.

teach.b: Japa. Repeating a mantra, or a name of God, again and again, often counted. That's what Dhruva does.
Month after month he keeps at it, and in the story Vishnu himself comes to the boy. Dhruva is given a kingdom, and in the end a place in the sky that never moves.
Hindus call the pole star by his name: Dhruva, the steady one. He got there not by one great prayer, but by one name, said again.
In the Gita, Krishna counts that as an offering: among offerings, I am japa. It needs no fire and no flowers.
That's why many Hindus receive a mantra from a guru, as Dhruva received his from Narada, and repeat it every day on a mala, a string of beads: one bead, one repetition.
By tradition a full mala carries a hundred and eight beads, plus one at the top that the fingers don't pass over. Why a hundred and eight?
People give answers from the sky, from lists of divine names, from the body; no text settles it, so we'll leave it open.

teach.h: COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.
teach.b: But a fixed count gives the practice an end. You know when you're done, and you can pick it up again tomorrow. That's how a prayer gets kept: not once, in a crisis, but every day, until it's as steady as the pole star.

how: Devotees do japa with a mala, moving one bead per repetition of a mantra or a divine name, often at a set time each day; some count on the sections of the fingers instead.

games.q: Nani gave me her old tulsi mala before she goes home 🥹 but i don't have a mantra?? do i just… count beads?
o: japa is a name or mantra, one bead each. Narada gave Dhruva his. ask Nani to give you one.
just count. the counting is the prayer.
wait until you can do all 108 perfectly, then start.
games.why: Narada gave Dhruva a mantra and Dhruva repeated it until Vishnu came. Japa is a mantra or name repeated, often received from a guru and counted on a mala.

games.q: match the story to the practice.
p: the boy pulled off his father's lap
the sage who gave him a mantra
the string of beads that keeps count
a mantra or name, said again

s: there's one agreed reason for the 108 beads
people give answers from the sky, from lists of names, from the body. no text settles it.
Dhruva got his mantra from the sage Narada
Narada gave him om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, and the boy repeated it by the Yamuna.
you need beads to do japa
the fingers work too: three sections a finger, the thumb as the counter.

games.q: you're halfway around a string of beads, and you start wondering whether you've done enough. what does the fixed count do for you?
o: nothing; keep going until it feels like enough.
it decides for you: you're done when the string ends.
it tells you to stop at halfway.
games.why: a fixed count gives the practice an end. you don't have to decide; the string decides, and tomorrow you can pick it up again.

practice: Here's the practice: count on your fingers. No beads needed. Each finger has three sections.
Touch your thumb to the top section of your index finger: one. The middle section: two. The base: three.
Then on to the next finger. With each touch, say om silently on the out-breath, or, if you pray, a name of God you use. Go slowly.
You won't reach a hundred and eight today, and Dhruva didn't start there either. The bell holds the time.

wordCard.voice: Japa. Repeating a mantra or a name, counted, so the hand keeps count and the mind can rest. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: quiet repetition of a mantra or a name of God.

carryVoice: Your line: count what you want to keep. Dhruva kept one name, again and again. Once today, count a few quiet repetitions on your fingers. Day thirteen.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 4.8–4.9 (Dhruva, Suruchi and Suniti; Narada gives the mantra, 4.8.54; Vishnu appears; Dhruva's fixed place)
